common_name: Purple Potion Trailing Lantana (Cascading Violet-Purple Groundcover Lantana)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Purple Potion is a trademarked selection of trailing lantana chosen for its rich violet-purple flower color and vigorous, dense cascading habit, making it well suited to raised beds, hanging baskets, and slope cover.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, medium-moisture soil in full sun after the last frost date; Purple Potion is a compact, low-mounding selection of trailing lantana with gray-green foliage and cascading stems that flow attractively over walls, raised beds, and hanging baskets rather than growing upright. It produces a near-continuous flush of rich violet-purple flower clusters with small white eyes from spring through fall, drawing butterflies steadily through the growing season. Like other trailing lantana selections, it is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the reflected heat of paving and hardscape where many other flowering groundcovers struggle. In zone 8, expect it to die back to the ground in a hard freeze and resprout from the roots the following spring; in zones 9-11 it remains evergreen to semi-evergreen and blooms nearly year-round.
sources: Monrovia — Purple Potion Trailing Lantana plant profile

common_name: Honeybells Cuphea (Compact Bicolor Rose-and-Yellow Hummingbird Cuphea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part sun; Honeybells is a patented hybrid cuphea bred for a tight, mounded habit and heavy, uninterrupted flowering without pinching, propagated by cuttings and sold only as nursery transplants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part sun after the last frost; Honeybells produces airy, bicolor tubular flowers in rose-pink with light yellow tips, held in loose sprays above a dense, mounded plant that stays notably tighter and more floriferous than seed-grown cuphea types. Bloom is continuous from late spring through the first hard frost with zero deadheading required, and the small tubular flower shape is precisely sized for hummingbird bills, making this one of the more effective hummingbird plants for containers and border edges in Gulf South heat. It performs equally well in ground beds or mixed containers, tolerating the high heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer without loss of vigor. Grown as a tender perennial in zone 9 and warmer, where it can persist as a small subshrub; treated as a warm-season annual farther north.
sources: Proven Winners — Honeybells Cuphea plant profile

common_name: Gold Edge Duranta (Variegated Gold-Margined Golden Dewdrop)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Gold Edge is an upright, variegated-foliage selection of Duranta erecta whose gold-margined leaves actually color best with some afternoon shade, unlike solid-gold cultivars that need full sun for peak color.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Gold Edge Duranta is grown chiefly for its foliage, with glossy green leaves broadly margined in bright gold that hold their variegation best when given some protection from the most intense midday sun. In frost-free climates it produces loose, lightly fragrant clusters of lavender-blue flowers with white-edged petals in mid-summer, followed by strings of small golden berries, though as a summer annual farther north it rarely flowers or fruits before frost ends the season. It grows considerably larger and more upright than compact golden-foliage cultivars like Gold Mound, reaching small-tree proportions where winters stay mild, so it works well as a specimen shrub, background planting, or trained standard. Where winters bring hard freezes it dies back to the ground and resprouts from the roots in spring, usually recovering its variegated color quickly once new growth emerges.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Duranta Cultivars for Florida

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March-May. Starla is a compact, uniform seed pentas series bred for a tidy, well-branched habit that stays shorter than older pentas types, making it a reliable choice for front-of-border and container plantings.

directions: Plant in full sun to light part shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Starla is a compact, early-flowering seed series of pentas available in red, lavender, deep rose, and white, each producing dense, domed clusters of five-petaled star-shaped flowers continuously from late spring through the first hard frost. Its shorter, well-branched habit stays tidier than older, taller pentas selections, holding a uniform mounded shape without pinching and making it dependable for mass bedding, edging, and container culture. Like all pentas, Starla performs best in the hottest, most humid stretch of a Gulf Coast summer, when many other bedding annuals decline, and its abundant, accessible flowers are a strong nectar source for butterflies, skippers, and hummingbirds. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom, though shearing lightly in mid-summer can refresh a leggy planting.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — GrowerFacts Pentas culture information
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pentas for Florida Landscapes

common_name: Orange Jubilee Tecoma (Large Golden-Orange Hybrid Yellow Bells)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean to average soil; Orange Jubilee is a large, fast-growing hybrid tecoma that can be trained as a multi-stemmed shrub, informal hedge, or espaliered vine depending on how it is pruned.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to average soil after the last frost; Orange Jubilee is a vigorous hybrid tecoma (Tecoma stans x Tecoma alata parentage) prized for large clusters of trumpet-shaped, golden-orange flowers that are noticeably showier and deeper colored than the yellow blooms of straight-species esperanza. It blooms heavily from spring through fall and is a strong hummingbird draw throughout the warm season. Fast-growing and considerably larger than compact tecoma hybrids, it can reach small-tree proportions where winters stay mild, so regular pruning helps keep it shrub-sized and densely branched for a landscape hedge or specimen planting. It is highly drought-tolerant once established; in zone 8, expect dieback to the ground in the coldest winters, with vigorous resprouting and a return to bloom by mid-summer.
sources: Arizona Municipal Water Users Association — low-water landscape plant database
